prerequisiteBridge: Electric charge may be positive or negative, and Coulomb force has both magnitude and direction. Potential energy U measures a system's capacity to do work at a position, with \(F=-\nabla U\); the minus sign means that the force points toward decreasing potential energy. Electric potential \(\phi =U/q\) is potential energy per unit charge, so the same potential difference produces opposite energy changes \(q\Delta \phi\) for positive and negative ions. Throughout this lecture, membrane voltage is defined as \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\): if the intracellular potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential, \(V_{m}=-60 \mathrm{mV}\). Begin every directional argument from this definition.

Diffusion arises from thermal motion in a nonuniform concentration: net particle flux runs from higher to lower concentration. If a membrane is permeable to only one ionic species, movement of a small number of ions separates charge across the membrane and creates an opposing electric field. At equilibrium, the chemical and electrical driving forces balance, so macroscopic net flux is zero even though individual ions continue to move in both directions. A logarithm converts a concentration ratio into an energy difference; an exponential converts that energy difference back into a concentration or probability ratio.

Only four circuit ideas are needed to begin: voltage is a difference in electric potential, current is the rate of charge flow \(I=dQ/dt\), a capacitor obeys \(Q=CV\), and a resistive branch can be written \(I=G(V-E)\), where \(G=1/R\). Unit conversion is crucial: \(1 \mathrm{pA}/1 \mathrm{pF}=1 \mathrm{V}/s\), and \(1 \mathrm{V}/s=1 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\). The positive current direction must be declared. Here, inward depolarizing current \(I_{e}\) enters the right-hand side positively, whereas outward ionic current \(G(V-E)\), which removes charge from the membrane capacitor, is subtracted.

The first-order time-constant analysis from the previous lecture applies directly. For \(\tau  dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), voltage approaches \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) exponentially from its initial value. A threshold–reset rule adds discrete events to that continuous trajectory. Understand the continuous voltage evolution and discrete spike events separately before combining them. The model does not reproduce an action-potential waveform; it represents a spike by the threshold-crossing time, an abstraction suited to studying spike timing and firing rate.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(V_{m}=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\), which side has the lower electric potential? On which side does a cation have lower electric potential energy?
diagnostic.answer: The intracellular electric potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential. For a cation with \(q>0\), \(U=q\phi\), so its electric potential energy is also lower inside.
diagnostic.explanation: First use the voltage definition to order the electric potentials, then multiply by the sign of the charge to order potential energies. The ordering reverses for anions, so “negative inside” alone cannot determine the direction of every ion.

diagnostic.prompt: Intracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration exceeds extracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration, and the Nernst equation uses \(\ln([K]_{\mathrm{out}}/[K]_{\mathrm{in}})\). Is the equilibrium potential positive or negative?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(z=+1\) and the concentration ratio is less than 1, the logarithm is negative; therefore \(E_{K}\) is negative.
diagnostic.explanation: The \(K^{+}\) concentration gradient drives efflux. Preventing net efflux requires a negative intracellular potential that attracts \(K^{+}\) inward, so the inside-minus-outside equilibrium potential is negative.

diagnostic.prompt: A membrane capacitor has \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\) and receives a constant inward current of 100 pA. Ignoring all ion channels, what is \(dV/dt\)?
diagnostic.explanation: The \(10^{-12}\) factors in pA/pF cancel to give V/s, whose numerical value equals mV/ms. A constant current therefore produces a linear voltage ramp across an ideal capacitor.

diagnostic.prompt: In a leaky integrate-and-fire model, \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). What minimum constant current places the subthreshold steady state exactly at threshold?
diagnostic.explanation: At threshold, \(dV/dt=0\) requires the applied current to exactly balance the leak current. Because \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), any smaller current leaves the steady state below threshold.

modules.title: Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium
modules.guidingQuestion: When an ion moves across a membrane down its concentration gradient, how does charge separation create an opposing electric field, and at what voltage does net flux vanish?
paragraphs: The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. The first page introduces the electrical sign convention through \(F=-\nabla U\) and \(\phi =U/q\), then defines \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\). A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams.

A concentration gradient supplies the diffusive drive. Suppose only \(K^{+}\) channels are open and \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}>[K]_{\mathrm{out}}\). Random motion produces net \(K^{+}\) efflux and leaves the inside relatively negative. As charge separation grows, the negative intracellular potential attracts \(K^{+}\) back inward. The chemical drive remains outward while the electrical drive points inward. At equilibrium, their contributions to the electrochemical-potential difference cancel, yielding zero net flux—not an end to microscopic ion exchange.

For a dilute solution, the molar electrochemical potential of an ion is \(\mu =\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c+zF\phi\). This is equivalent to the single-particle Boltzmann form in the source: \(q_{c}=z e\), \(R=N_{Ak,B}\), and \(F=N_{Ae}\), so \(RT/(zF)=k_{\mathrm{BT}}/q_{c}\). At equilibrium, \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}=\exp(q_{c}E/k_{\mathrm{BT}})\); taking the logarithm gives \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_{\mathrm{out}}=(RT/zF)\ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\). For a cation, \(z>0\) preserves the logarithm's sign. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses it.

An equilibrium potential is not the voltage that a membrane must have at every instant. It is the voltage at which the net current carried by one ionic species is zero. Away from \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\), current direction depends on the driving force \(V_{m}-E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) together with channel conductance. The source values—about +55 mV for \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), −75 mV for \(K^{+}\), +125 mV for \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), and −60 mV for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\)—are illustrative physiological values, not universal constants. Nernst potentials vary with concentration, temperature, and activity, while the actual \(V_{m}\) depends on multiple permeabilities and dynamic gating.

This framework also explains the direction of an action-potential trajectory. Rapid Na⁺-channel opening pulls \(V_{m}\) toward the positive \(E_{\mathrm{Na}}\). \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) inactivation and a delayed rise in \(K^{+}\) conductance then pull \(V_{m}\) back toward \(E_{K}\), after which channel recovery and leak currents return the membrane to rest. Approaching a reversal potential does not instantaneously equalize ion concentrations: only a small fraction of the cellular ion reservoir crosses the membrane during one action potential.
keyPoints: Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral.
Nernst equilibrium is a zero-net-flux state in which chemical and electrical driving forces cancel.
The sign of \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is set jointly by the definition \(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_{\mathrm{out}}\), the concentration ratio, and the signed valence z.
A reversal potential is the zero-current voltage for one ionic branch, not the membrane voltage at every instant.

derivation.title: From the Boltzmann ratio on the source page to the Nernst equation
derivation.setup: Assume that the membrane is permeable to a single ionic species with charge \(q_{c}=z e\), that temperature T is constant, and that the solutions on both sides are approximately ideal and dilute. At equilibrium, the electrochemical occupancies are compatible and net transmembrane flux is zero.

steps.title: Write the Boltzmann weight used on the source page
steps.explanation: The probability of a state decreases exponentially with its potential energy; the electric potential energy of one ion is its charge times the local electric potential.

steps.title: Relate the occupancy ratio to the concentration ratio
steps.explanation: The equilibrium occupancy of the same ion on the two sides is represented by their concentration ratio, with the transmembrane potential difference entering the exponent.

steps.title: Write the electrochemical potential on each side
steps.explanation: The two sides have \(\mu _{\mathrm{in}}=\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c_{\mathrm{in}}+zF\phi _{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(\mu _{\mathrm{out}}=\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c_{\mathrm{out}}+zF\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\), respectively.

steps.title: Connect single-particle and molar notation
steps.explanation: Using \(q_{c}=z e\), \(R=N_{Ak,B}\), and \(F=N_{Ae}\), divide molar energy by Avogadro's constant to obtain \(RT/(zF)=k_{\mathrm{BT}}/q_{c}\). Thus, the source's Boltzmann concentration ratio and the molar Nernst equation express the same physical equilibrium in two unit systems.

steps.title: Impose electrochemical equilibrium
steps.explanation: Zero net flux corresponds to \(\mu _{\mathrm{in}}=\mu _{\mathrm{out}}\). The standard chemical potential \(\mu ^{0}\) is identical for the same ion on both sides, so rearrangement gives \(zF(\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}})=RT \ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\).

steps.title: Insert the membrane-voltage definition
steps.explanation: Use \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\) and denote the equilibrium membrane voltage for this ion by \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\).

steps.title: Solve for the equilibrium potential
steps.explanation: Dividing by zF yields \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=(RT/zF)\ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\). Because valence appears in the denominator, a divalent ion has half the voltage magnitude of a monovalent ion at the same concentration ratio.

steps.title: Connect the result to current direction
steps.explanation: Under a linear conductance approximation, \(I_{\mathrm{ion}}=G_{\mathrm{ion}}(V_{m}-E_{\mathrm{ion}})\). Current through this branch is zero at \(V_{m}=E_{\mathrm{ion}}\); away from that voltage, the sign gives the direction under the stated convention.

symbolNotes: \(N_{A}\) is Avogadro's constant, and e is the positive magnitude of the elementary charge. The signed valence z carries the sign of ionic charge, so \(q_{c}=z e\).
\(k_{B}\) and \(q_{c}\) are per-particle quantities; R and F are per-mole quantities. Do not mix the two notation systems.

\(c_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{out}}\) are the intracellular and extracellular activities, or approximate concentrations, of the same ion. They must use the same units so that their ratio is dimensionless.
The valence z includes its sign: +1 for \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) and \(K^{+}\), +2 for \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), and −1 for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\).
\(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) uses inside potential minus outside potential. Reversing the voltage definition reverses the overall sign of the formula.
derivation.unitsCheck: RT has units J/mol and F has units C/mol, so \(RT/F=J/C=V\). The concentration ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless; \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is measured in volts.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(c_{\mathrm{out}}=c_{\mathrm{in}}\), the logarithm is zero and \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=0\). Increasing \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}\) for a cation makes \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) more positive. The ideal formula tends toward zero voltage as \(T\to 0\), but a physiological model is not valid at absolute zero.

workedExample.title: Calculate the \(K^{+}\) equilibrium potential at body temperature
workedExample.problem: Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM.
steps: The initial concentration ratio is \(5/140\approx 0.035714\), and \(\ln(0.035714)\approx -3.332\).
After extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises, the ratio is \(10/140\approx 0.071429\) and its logarithm is ≈−2.639.
The new value is \(E_{K}\approx 26.7\cdot (-2.639)=-70.46 \mathrm{mV}\), about 18.5 mV more positive than before—a depolarizing shift.
workedExample.result: Initially \(E_{K}\approx -89 \mathrm{mV}\); doubling extracellular \(K^{+}\) shifts \(E_{K}\) to ≈−70.5 mV.
workedExample.sanityCheck: In both cases \(c_{\mathrm{out}}<c_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(z>0\), so \(E_{K}\) must be negative. Raising the external concentration moves the ratio toward 1 and reduces the magnitude of the potential.

selfCheck.prompt: If \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of \(K^{+}\)?
selfCheck.answer: In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge.

pitfalls: Mixing \([ion]_{\mathrm{in}}/[ion]_{\mathrm{out}}\) with \([ion]_{\mathrm{out}}/[ion]_{\mathrm{in}}\) without changing the sign to match the voltage convention.
Using \(z=+1\) for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) and thereby obtaining an equilibrium potential with the wrong sign.
Interpreting zero net flux as no microscopic exchange, or interpreting a reversal potential as equal concentrations.

modules.title: The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL
modules.guidingQuestion: How does each biological membrane feature map onto a circuit element, and how does charge conservation combine those elements into a membrane-voltage equation?
paragraphs: The lipid bilayer separates conducting solutions and allows opposite charges to accumulate on its inner and outer surfaces, so it acts as a capacitor C. Ion channels provide selective conducting pathways; the number of open channels and their single-channel conductance combine into a conductance G. Each ion's concentration gradient sets a reversal potential E, represented by a battery in series with the conductance. An external electrode or synaptic input injects charge and is represented by a current source \(I_{e}\). This equivalent circuit preserves relationships among charge flow and voltage; it does not claim that the membrane contains metal components.

For fixed C, \(Q=CV\) means that changing voltage requires changing surface charge. Differentiating gives \(dQ/dt=C dV/dt\), and the definition \(I=dQ/dt\) therefore gives \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\). Injecting 100 pA into a 200 pF capacitor produces a slope of 0.5 mV/ms. A capacitor alone does not set a steady state: as long as a nonzero constant net current persists, voltage continues to change linearly.

Under a linear conductance approximation, an ionic branch obeys \(I_{x}=G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\). Net current is zero at \(V_{m}=E_{x}\), and the driving force grows with the distance from \(E_{x}\). \(G_{x}\) may be constant, as for a passive leak \(G_{L}\), or vary with voltage and time, as do \(G_{\mathrm{Na}}(t,V)\) and \(G_{K}(t,V)\) in the Hodgkin–Huxley model. The battery \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage; conductance determines the current produced by a given driving force.

Apply Kirchhoff's current law at the membrane node: net current entering the capacitor equals applied current minus the outward ionic currents, giving C \(dV_{m}/dt=I_{e}-\sum _x G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\). Every term has units of current. A positive net sum deposits positive charge on the inner capacitor plate and raises \(V_{m}\); a negative sum lowers \(V_{m}\); a zero sum makes voltage momentarily stationary. This equation is the common backbone of the IF, LIF, and Hodgkin–Huxley models.

The Hodgkin–Huxley equivalent circuit on the third page contains the membrane capacitor, a leak branch, and variable Na and K branches. Conductance changes during an action potential make those branches compete: increasing \(G_{\mathrm{Na}}\) pulls V more strongly toward \(E_{\mathrm{Na}}\), whereas increasing \(G_{K}\) pulls V toward \(E_{K}\). “Pull toward” does not mean setting voltage instantaneously to a reversal potential; capacitance and every other open branch determine the rate and trajectory.
keyPoints: The lipid membrane maps to capacitance, ion channels to conductance, and concentration gradients to reversal-potential batteries.
KCL combines applied current and all ionic branches into one voltage-dynamics equation.
Conductance sets the strength of attraction toward a reversal potential; capacitance sets how quickly voltage can change.

derivation.title: Derive the multichannel membrane equation from charge conservation
derivation.setup: The membrane has capacitance C, receives an applied current \(I_{e}\) defined as positive inward, and contains several ionic branches. Define branch current from inside to outside as \(I_{x}=G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\).

steps.title: Relate charge to voltage
steps.explanation: The relative charge on the inner membrane surface is \(Q=C V_{m}\). Assuming that C is constant, \(dQ/dt=C dV_{m}/dt\).

steps.title: Write conservation at the node
steps.explanation: The rate of increase of intracellular surface charge equals inward applied current \(I_{e}\) minus all branch currents flowing from inside to outside.

steps.title: Solve the constant-conductance steady state
steps.explanation: If every \(G_{x}\) is constant, set \(dV/dt=0\) and rearrange to obtain \(V^{*}= [I_{e}+\sum _x G_{x} E_{x}]/\sum _x G_{x}\): a conductance-weighted reversal potential plus the offset caused by applied current.

steps.title: Identify the time scale
steps.explanation: With total conductance \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum G_{x}\), write the equation as \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V^{*}\), where \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\). Opening more channels therefore shortens the time constant.

symbolNotes: By convention, positive \(I_{e}\) injects positive charge into the cell, while positive \(I_{x}\) carries positive charge from inside to outside.
\(G_{x}\ge 0\) is branch conductance and \(E_{x}\) is that ion's reversal potential; \(G_{x}(V-E_{x})\) may be positive or negative.
C is total membrane capacitance. If parameters are expressed per unit area, divide every term in the equation by membrane area.
derivation.unitsCheck: C·dV/dt has units \(F\cdot V/s=C/s=A\), and G·(V−E) has units \(S\cdot V=A\), so every term can be added in one KCL equation.
derivation.limitCheck: If all \(G_{x}=0\), the equation reduces to the ideal capacitor \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no finite steady state. If one \(G_{k}\) greatly exceeds all other conductances while \(I_{e}\) remains finite, \(V^{*}\) approaches \(E_{k}\).

workedExample.title: Instantaneous slope and steady state of a two-branch membrane
workedExample.problem: Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\).
steps: The outward K current is \(20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+85)\mathrm{mV}=500 \mathrm{pA}\), so net inward current is \(300-50-500=-250 \mathrm{pA}\).
Thus \(dV/dt=-250 \mathrm{pA}/200 \mathrm{pF}=-1.25 \mathrm{V}/s=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\), so voltage is falling at this instant.
Total conductance is 30 nS, so \(V^{*}=-2050/30 \mathrm{mV}\approx -68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(\tau =C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}=200 \mathrm{pF}/30 \mathrm{nS}\approx 6.67 \mathrm{ms}\).
workedExample.result: At −60 mV, \(dV/dt=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\); the steady state is approximately −68.3 mV and the time constant is approximately 6.67 ms.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The steady state should reflect competition among the two branches after the current-induced shift. Substituting \(V=-68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) makes the total outward branch current approximately 300 pA.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach?
selfCheck.answer: It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\), which reduces the membrane time constant \(C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\); voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster.

pitfalls: Memorizing C dV/dt without declaring current directions, then mixing sign conventions across ionic branches.
Treating reversal potential E as if conductance created it. E comes from an electrochemical gradient; G sets current magnitude.
Forgetting that \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), or reporting pA/pF as mV/s instead of V/s or mV/ms.

modules.title: From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire
modules.guidingQuestion: What firing behavior follows from threshold and reset alone, and why does adding a leak branch create a steady state, a rheobase current, and a nonlinear F–I curve?
paragraphs: The perfect integrate-and-fire model retains capacitance C and applied current \(I_{e}\), with subthreshold equation \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\). A constant positive current produces a linear ramp with slope \(I_{e}/C\). When V reaches threshold \(V_{T}\), the model records a spike and resets V to \(V_{R}\). Spike times stand in for action potentials; the model does not reproduce waveforms generated by Na and K conductances. It converts input current into interspike intervals but has no resting attractor.

Moving from \(V_{R}\) to \(V_{T}\) requires \(\Delta V=V_{T}-V_{R}\). Under constant current, the ramp time is \(\Delta t=C\Delta V/I_{e}\), so without a refractory period \(f=1/\Delta t=I_{e}/[C(V_{T}-V_{R})]\). Every \(I_{e}>0\) eventually produces a spike, so the perfect model has no positive rheobase current and its F–I curve rises linearly from the origin. Real neurons, by contrast, may remain at rest under a weak constant input.

Adding a leak branch gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Leak grows with the displacement of V from \(E_{L}\) and always pulls voltage toward \(E_{L}\). With \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\), the equation becomes \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant input, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\); voltage approaches a finite steady state exponentially instead of rising without bound.

Spiking requires \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) to lie above threshold. The boundary condition \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=V_{T}\) gives \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). If \(I_{e}\le I_{T}\), the steady state remains subthreshold and sustained current produces no periodic spikes. If \(I_{e}>I_{T}\), the exponential solution gives the travel time from \(V_{R}\) to \(V_{T}\). This threshold current emerges from the balance between input and leak; it is not an extra current rule inserted by hand.

LIF still omits the action-potential waveform, channel gating, adaptation, and absolute refractoriness, but it links biophysical circuit elements to spike events. Compare models term by term: perfect IF and LIF both contain capacitance, threshold, and reset; only LIF contains \(E_{L}\), \(G_{L}\), a finite steady state, and a positive rheobase. Identifying the responsible term lets you interpret an F–I change as a mechanistic consequence.
keyPoints: Perfect IF ramps linearly under constant current; every positive current eventually produces a spike.
Threshold and reset are event rules, not a simulation of the action-potential waveform.

derivation.title: LIF steady state, rheobase, and first-spike time
derivation.setup: Consider \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\) with constant \(I_{e}\), initial voltage \(V(0)=V_{R}\), and threshold \(V_{T}>V_{R}\).

steps.title: Define the time constant and steady state
steps.explanation: Rewrite the right-hand side as \(-G_{L}[V-(E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L})]\), then define \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\).

steps.title: Write the subthreshold solution
steps.explanation: This is a first-order linear system with steady state \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), so \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{R}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})\exp(-t/\tau _{m})\).

steps.title: Obtain the rheobase current
steps.explanation: A trajectory starting below threshold can cross only if \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\). The boundary \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=V_{T}\) gives \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\).

steps.title: Take the logarithm
steps.explanation: When \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}>V_{R}\), the ratio lies between 0 and 1, giving \(t_{sp}=\tau _{m} \ln[(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})]\). Without a refractory period, the periodic firing rate is \(1/t_{sp}\).

symbolNotes: \(V_{R}\) is the reset voltage after each spike and \(V_{T}\) is the event threshold; neither is an ionic reversal potential.
\(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) is the constant-input steady state of the subthreshold equation when reset is disabled.
\(\tau _{m}\) is capacitance divided by leak conductance. Increasing capacitance slows the response; increasing conductance speeds it up.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(C/G_{L}\) has units \(F/S=s\); \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units \(A/S=V\); the logarithm contains a dimensionless ratio of voltage differences; \(t_{sp}\) is a time.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\) from above, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T}\to 0\), \(t_{sp}\to \infty\), and firing \(\mathrm{rate}\to 0\). For very large \(I_{e}\), leak matters less during the short ramp and the result approaches the perfect-IF value \(C(V_{T}-V_{R})/I_{e}\).

workedExample.title: Compare subthreshold behavior and repetitive firing with the same parameters
workedExample.problem: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period.
steps: The membrane time constant is \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}=200 \mathrm{pF}/10 \mathrm{nS}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), and the rheobase is \(I_{T}=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\).
At 100 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65 \mathrm{mV}+100 \mathrm{pA}/10 \mathrm{nS}=-55 \mathrm{mV}\), below −50 mV, so the trajectory never crosses threshold.
At 200 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65+20=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), above threshold. The threshold-time ratio is \((V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})=20/5=4\).
Therefore \(t_{sp}=20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot \ln 4\approx 20\cdot 1.3863=27.73 \mathrm{ms}\). Each reset returns to the same voltage under the same input, so every cycle has the same duration.
workedExample.result: At 100 pA, voltage approaches −55 mV without spiking. At 200 pA, the first interval is about 27.7 ms and the repetitive rate is about 36.1 Hz.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Because 200 pA is only slightly above the 150 pA rheobase, the rate should be finite and modest. Ignoring leak, perfect IF gives \(15 \mathrm{mV}/(1 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms})=15 \mathrm{ms}\), correctly predicting a faster crossing.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above?
selfCheck.answer: Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold.
